learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells: Next-Gen Efficiency
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells are revolutionizing photovoltaics with their rapid efficiency gains and low-cost manufacturing potential. These emerging materials could soon surpass traditional silicon cells, offering a brighter, more sustainable future for solar energy worldwide.
learn.c1_text: Perovskite solar cells have seen their efficiency jump from under 4% in 2009 to over 30% today. This dramatic improvement rivals decades of silicon development, making them a promising contender for next-generation solar technology.
learn.c2_text: Unlike silicon, perovskites can be printed using simple solution-based techniques, slashing production costs. This method resembles printing newspapers—fast, scalable, and far cheaper than high-temperature silicon fabrication.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 500 GW renewable capacity by 2030. Perovskite-silicon tandem cells could help achieve this by boosting rooftop and utility-scale output without expanding land use—a critical advantage for densely populated regions.
learn.stat1: Perovskite cell efficiency reached 33% in lab tests (2024)
learn.stat2: Silicon cells dominate 95% of global PV market
learn.stat3: Perovskite production cost estimated at $0.10/W by 2030
learn.stat4: India plans 500 GW renewable capacity by 2030

learn.title: Levelised Cost of Energy Explained
learn.intro: The Levelised Cost of Energy (LCOE) is the key metric for comparing power sources fairly. It accounts for total lifetime costs, helping policymakers and investors make informed decisions about which technologies deliver the most value over time.
learn.c1_text: LCOE calculates the average cost per megawatt-hour of electricity generated over a plant’s lifetime. Think of it like comparing cars not just by sticker price but by total fuel, maintenance, and resale value over years of driving.
learn.c2_text: LCOE includes capital, operating, and fuel costs divided by total energy output. It reveals true competitiveness—like discovering your electric car saves money over gas when factoring in maintenance and fuel prices over five years.
learn.c3_text: India’s solar LCOE dropped 89% since 2010, reaching ₹1.99/kWh in 2023. This makes solar cheaper than coal in many regions, accelerating India’s clean energy transition and reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels.
learn.stat1: Solar LCOE fell 89% in India since 2010

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels Power Both Sides
learn.intro: Bifacial solar panels capture sunlight from both sides, increasing energy yield by up to 30%. As solar adoption grows, these innovative panels offer a smart upgrade for maximizing output in limited spaces like rooftops and solar farms.
learn.c1_text: Bifacial panels generate power from their front and rear sides by capturing reflected light from surfaces like snow, sand, or white roofs. This design can boost energy production like adding a second solar panel without extra space.
learn.c2_text: Field studies show bifacial panels produce 10–30% more energy than traditional monofacial ones. The gain depends on installation height, ground reflectivity, and tracking systems—making them ideal for open, reflective environments.
learn.c3_text: India’s National Solar Mission promotes bifacial panels in large-scale projects. The Bhadla Solar Park uses bifacial modules to enhance output across Rajasthan’s sunny, sandy terrain, improving ROI for developers and discoms alike.
learn.stat1: Bifacial panels increase yield by up to 30%
learn.stat2: Global bifacial module shipments hit 20 GW in 2023
learn.stat4: Bhadla Solar Park spans 14,000 acres in Rajasthan

learn.title: India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission
learn.intro: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to position the country as a global leader in clean hydrogen production. With massive investment and ambitious targets, this initiative could transform heavy industry and transportation while creating millions of jobs.
learn.c1_text: Launched in 2023, the mission targets 5 MMT of green hydrogen production annually by 2030. This equals powering over 120 million homes for a year—equivalent to replacing 200 million tons of coal in steel, fertilizer, and transport sectors.
learn.c2_text: The mission plans to attract $2.3 billion in investment and create 300,000 jobs. Green hydrogen will decarbonize industries that can’t easily use batteries, like steelmaking and shipping—key steps toward India’s net-zero 2070 goal.
learn.c3_text: Reliance Industries and NTPC are building mega green hydrogen hubs in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. These projects align with India’s 500 GW renewables target, leveraging surplus solar and wind power to produce low-cost green hydrogen at scale.

learn.title: Concentrated Solar Power with Mirrors
learn.intro: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) uses mirrors to focus sunlight and generate intense heat, driving turbines to produce electricity—even after sunset. Unlike rooftop solar, CSP can store energy and provide reliable power day and night.
learn.c1_text: CSP plants store heat in molten salt or other materials, releasing it later to generate electricity. This is like charging a thermal battery with sunlight—enabling power generation even when the sun sets or clouds roll in.
learn.c2_text: CSP thrives in arid regions with high direct normal irradiance (DNI). Mirrors called heliostats track the sun, focusing rays onto a central receiver. This setup can achieve temperatures exceeding 1,000°C—hot enough to melt steel.
learn.c3_text: India has identified 21 CSP sites with DNI above 6 kWh/m²/day. The 125 MW Dhursar plant in Rajasthan demonstrates CSP’s viability. With hybrid storage, CSP supports grid stability as India scales up its renewable ambitions.
learn.stat1: CSP can store energy for up to 15 hours

learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV)
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) seamlessly blend solar technology into building materials like roofs, facades, and windows. This dual-purpose approach turns structures into power generators, saving space and transforming urban skylines into clean energy assets.
learn.c1_text: BIPV replaces conventional building materials with solar-generating ones—like solar roof tiles or tinted glass panels that double as windows. This eliminates the need for separate mounting systems, reducing both cost and visual impact.
learn.c2_text: BIPV maximizes limited urban space by turning walls and rooftops into energy sources. A typical office building with BIPV facade can generate enough power to run lighting and elevators—cutting grid dependence and carbon emissions significantly.
learn.c3_text: India’s Energy Conservation Building Code encourages BIPV in commercial constructions. The CIS Tower in Mumbai features integrated solar panels, showcasing how metros can meet rising power demand while cutting emissions through smart urban design.
learn.stat1: BIPV market to reach $38.2 billion by 2030
